checkpoints: KEYS[1] is the stock key, declared via KEYS (never hardcoded in the script body) so it still routes correctly on Redis Cluster.
ARGV[1] is the requested amount.
The script returns a structured result shaped like [ok, remaining, reason] with reason in {OK, OUT_OF_STOCK, INVALID}, so the caller can branch instead of guessing the meaning of a bare number.

The whole read — check — decrement lives inside the script as ONE atomic critical section, so two reservation requests for the same SKU arriving at once can't both read 'enough stock' and both decrement — no oversell.

MULTI/EXEC can't replace this because it only batches several commands into one round trip; it doesn't let you read a value and then branch logic mid-transaction — Lua runs if/else server-side based on the value it just GETs.
The client-side contract loads the script once with SCRIPT LOAD to get a SHA, then calls it via EVALSHA.
On a NOSCRIPT error (Redis restart/cache flush) the client falls back to EVAL and retries.
Names the tagging granularity as per-entity — {user:<id>} or {tenant:<id>} — not a global tag.
States that every key belonging to the same user/tenant carries the identical bracketed tag (e.g. {user:42}.profile, {user:42}.cart, {user:42}.counters).
Explains Redis Cluster's slot formula hashes ONLY the substring inside {...} (CRC16 of that substring mod 16384), not the whole key.
Concludes that a shared tag forces same-node placement (one slot), which is what lets a Lua script/MULTI touch all those keys atomically without a CROSSSLOT error.
States that keys from different users/tenants must NOT share a tag, so they still spread across the 16384 slots for load distribution.
Explains that an overly broad tag (e.g. {global}) collapses the whole keyspace onto a single slot, creating a hot slot that a reshard cannot split further (slot is the smallest movable unit).
Frames the explicit trade-off: narrower tag scope → easier atomicity but less co-located data per operation; broader tag scope → larger atomic scope but worse load distribution.
Concludes {user:<id>}/{tenant:<id>} is the right balance for multi-tenant: avoids a hot slot while still covering the multi-key ops that must be atomic.
The cluster splits the keyspace into a fixed 16384 hash slots, and each master owns a contiguous range of them.
When the 4th node joins, the cluster reshards by moving a range of already-existing slots to the new master — no key is rehashed in the process.
That's because slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384 is a pure function of the key, completely independent of how many nodes currently exist, so every other key stays exactly where it was, untouched.
Application-layer sharding with hash(userId) % nodeCount is the opposite: changing N from 3 to 4 flips nearly every % N result at once, forcing mass key movement and triggering a cache-miss storm.
That approach also requires every service to atomically agree on the new N — if even one service lags behind, it computes a different node for the same key than everyone else.
Even after resharding completes, a multi-key or atomic operation still only runs correctly when both keys land in the same slot.
That constraint is exactly why hash tags — co-locating related keys into one slot — become necessary once you move to a cluster.
Requirement (a), finding articles tagged both "sports" and "hanoi", is an intersection between two groups, so use a set: SADD adds a member into a hashtable at O(1).
SINTER computes the intersection right on the server, instead of pulling both sets into the app and writing a loop to compare them.
Requirement (b), a user profile edited one field at a time, is a per-field write, so use a hash: HSET updates that exact field directly.
Requirement (c), a "latest 50 activities" feed, is a bounded time-ordered window, so use a list: LPUSH pushes the newest activity onto the head at O(1).
LTRIM feed:key 0 49 after every push keeps the list from growing without bound.

Wrong pick — stuffing the whole profile as a JSON string instead of a hash forces reading the whole object, parsing it, editing the field, and rewriting the entire blob for every single-field edit, wasting CPU and inviting a race when two requests edit at once.
Wrong pick — using a list for membership checks forces an LRANGE-then-loop in the app (O(N)) and also permits duplicates, since a list has no built-in dedup the way a set does.

EVALSHA turns "ship the whole script body every call" into "ship only a 40-character SHA1 of a script already SCRIPT LOADed", which matters cumulatively for a service calling the script on every transaction.
The script cache that SCRIPT LOAD writes to lives server-side on Redis, while the client holds only the SHA, a pointer into that cache.
When Redis restarts or the cache is flushed, the server-side cache goes back to empty, but the client has no idea and still assumes the old SHA is valid.
Calling EVALSHA with that stale SHA returns a NOSCRIPT error, even though nothing is wrong with the Lua logic itself.
A correct client must specifically catch NOSCRIPT and fall back by calling EVAL, sending the full script, which also reloads it into Redis' cache as a side effect.
After that fallback, the client returns to using EVALSHA as normal from the next call on, and many client libraries implement this fallback automatically.
For a rarely-called script, the bandwidth saved doesn't offset the cost of managing the SHA cache and writing the fallback logic — EVALSHA only pays off on genuinely high-frequency call paths.
MOVED means slot ownership has moved permanently to another node, so the client durably updates its cached slot-table.
After a MOVED update, all subsequent traffic for that slot goes straight to the new node without needing to ask again.
ASK happens when a slot is mid-migration, with part of its keys already on the destination and the rest still on the source.
ASK only redirects the current command to the destination once and deliberately leaves the cache untouched, because nothing has settled yet.

If the client treated ASK exactly like MOVED, overwriting the cache the moment it sees ASK, every subsequent command for that slot would be sent straight to the destination regardless of whether a given key had actually moved.
That would misroute the not-yet-moved keys still sitting on the source right in the middle of the migration — a correctness bug, not a performance one.

Keeping MOVED (settled) strictly apart from ASK (in transit) is what lets resharding happen with zero downtime — every command during migration is routed correctly for its specific key, while the cache is only permanently updated once the whole slot has truly settled on the new node.
A stream is the correct structure: XADD key * lets Redis auto-generate a monotonically increasing timestamp-seq ID that faithfully reflects the order events actually happened in.
An entry stays in the stream after it's been read — it is not deleted the way a normal queue would delete it.
A stream supports consumer groups: multiple workers can read the same stream while splitting the work, with each entry delivered to only one worker within the group.
Each worker/group keeps its own offset, so reading from the start again — after a redeploy, a crashed worker, or an audit — just means replaying from an older offset or from the very beginning.
A list has no ID attached to elements and no per-consumer offset — LPUSH/RPOP work fine for a plain FIFO queue.
But once an element is popped from a list it is gone forever: nobody can replay it, and there's no way for multiple workers to split the work without stepping on each other.

A sorted set orders members by a caller-chosen score (a rank, an expiry time, a priority) rather than by write order, and has no consumer-group concept whatsoever — using it to track "who has read up to where" means bolting on ad-hoc logic outside Redis, the wrong tool for the job.

If the problem is just a lightweight FIFO with nobody needing replay or group fan-out, a plain list is simpler and cheaper — only pay for the stream's machinery when those specific capabilities are actually needed.

Redis Cluster decides which node executes a Lua script solely from the keys declared in `KEYS[]`; it hashes each declared key to one of 16384 hash slots and requires every `KEYS[]` entry to map to the same slot before it will route and run the script.
`ARGV[]` values play no part in Cluster's routing decision — only keys passed through `KEYS[]` are hashed to pick which node runs the script.

Calling `evalsha`/`eval` with `numkeys` set to 0 declares zero keys, so Cluster has nothing to hash or route on; depending on the client, the call either errors immediately or gets forwarded to whatever node the connection last happened to be talking to.

Hardcoding key names as string literals inside the Lua script body (e.g. `redis.call("GET", "acct:src")`) bypasses `KEYS[]` entirely — the script still touches those literal keys once it executes somewhere, but Cluster never saw them at routing time.

Two independently-named keys such as `acct:src` and `acct:dst` can hash to different slots that live on different nodes; whichever node the script lands on, a `GET`/`DECRBY`/`INCRBY` against a key that isn't local to that node either triggers a `CROSSSLOT` error or, depending on client/proxy behavior, silently reads or writes the wrong node's data.

A single-node Redis instance has no hash slots and performs no `CROSSSLOT` check at all, so a script with hardcoded keys and `numkeys=0` runs and returns correct results there — completely hiding the bug until the identical script and call are pointed at a real Cluster.

The fix is to declare every key the script touches through `KEYS[1]`/`KEYS[2]` instead of literals in the body, and to pass the matching count as `numkeys` in the call, e.g. `redis.evalsha(sha, 2, key1, key2, ...args)`.

Naming two related keys with a shared hash tag — the portion wrapped in curly braces, e.g. `acct:{wallet}:src` and `acct:{wallet}:dst` — makes Cluster hash only the text inside `{}`, forcing both keys onto the same slot regardless of which node receives the call, which is what lets a multi-key script run atomically on Cluster.
A Redis list is a doubly-linked list with no by-value index, so answering "is this value already in the list" requires scanning every element one by one - an O(N) operation.
LPUSH (or RPUSH) has no concept of uniqueness and always adds the value unconditionally, so nothing stops the same user id from being pushed onto the list multiple times, producing duplicate likes.

Redis executes commands on a single thread, so a full-collection read like `LRANGE key 0 -1` on a large, hot key is an O(N) command that must finish packing and returning every element before Redis can serve any other client - it blocks all other requests, even unrelated ones, for its entire duration.
The real fix is a data-structure change, not a smarter loop: model "likes" as a Redis set instead of a list.
A set is backed by a hashtable, so both membership checks (`SISMEMBER`) and inserts (`SADD`) are O(1), regardless of how many elements the set holds.

`SADD` is idempotent - adding the same user id any number of times still leaves exactly one entry - so the separate check-then-push step becomes unnecessary; a single `SADD key userId` call is enough to both add and dedupe.

If the set can grow very large and the full membership list is occasionally needed, reading it all at once with `SMEMBERS` reintroduces the same single-thread-blocking problem as `LRANGE`; iterating with cursor-based `SSCAN` in small batches avoids monopolizing Redis.

Correct behavior can be verified by calling the like action twice with the same user id and asserting the set's cardinality (`SCARD`) stays at 1 rather than growing, and by confirming the membership check no longer issues any full-collection read command.

Routing that computes `hash(key) % nodeCount` ties node assignment to the current node count, so adding or removing a node changes the divisor and shifts nearly every key's remainder to a different node — a scaling event turns into a mass key-movement that triggers a cache-miss storm exactly when the system needs to stay stable.

Nothing in a plain hash-mod-N scheme guarantees that two related keys for the same entity (a profile and a cart, say) land on the same node, and that guarantee holds even less once the node count changes — so cross-key operations like MULTI, a Lua script, or MGET cannot be trusted to touch a single node atomically.

Hardcoding the hash function and the node list inside one helper means every other service that needs the same routing has to copy that exact logic; any drift between copies — a different hash constant, a different node order — causes one service to silently read or write the wrong node for a key another service considers correct.

Real Redis Cluster replaces `% nodeCount` with a fixed 16384-slot keyspace: keys map to slots via CRC16, and the client caches a slot-to-node table (built from `CLUSTER SLOTS`) so routing happens without any hand-written modulo logic.

Because the slot count never depends on the node count, adding or removing a node under Redis Cluster only moves the specific slot ranges reassigned to it — a reshard proportional to the change — instead of reshuffling the entire keyspace the way mod-N routing does.

Hash tags such as `{user:1}.profile` and `{user:1}.cart` force related keys into the same slot by hashing only the substring inside the braces, which is what makes multi-key atomic operations safe under Redis Cluster.

Splitting a PR review into must-fix correctness/availability defects (unbounded rehash on scale, broken cross-key atomicity) versus lower-priority cleanup (like extracting the duplicated pickNode logic into a shared module) matters because deduplicating the helper does not fix the underlying architecture — only moving to a real cluster resolves the root cause.

The mod-N scaling problem is demonstrable concretely: adding a fourth node to a 3-node mod-N setup remaps roughly 70-80% of the keyspace to different nodes, whereas Redis Cluster under the same change only migrates the specific slot ranges reassigned, leaving the rest of the keyspace untouched.
